The tally showed that 37 percent voted against it and 7.4 percent abstained, Cornell University spokesperson Rebecca Valli said.

Her lawsuit, filed in September, has also drawn criticism of the university’s handling of the case in 2024. Cornell, located in Ithaca, New York, responded that it had conducted a comprehensive investigation and imposed disciplinary measures, including expulsions.

sources.text:
On Friday, November 6, Cornell University’s faculty placed a vote of no confidence in the university’s administration amid heavy criticism of its handling of a sexual assault allegation involving a former student who has only been identified as Jane Doe. The former student has alleged that she was drugged with ketamine and gang-raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity at a fraternity house in 2024.
The Senate Has ‘No Confidence’ In The Ability To Address The ‘Ongoing Crisis’ At Cornell
Cornell’s University faculty passed the resolution on Friday, November 6, with 75 members voting in favor and 50 voting against. Only five members abstained, according to the university’s official website. The resolution states that the Senate “has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University.”
“The faculty co-sponsors of this resolution deliberated at great length on this resolution,” the statement continued. “As you may suspect, we were approached in our capacity as faculty senators by numerous Cornell colleagues demanding action. Many of these faculty–including myself–were approached by students at Cornell who are upset, fearful for their personal safety, and wanting our university to address the perennial problem of sexual assault on the campus.”
“Cornell alumni, some of whom have shared their own traumatic stories as students, have also contacted faculty to share their frustrations about this matter,” they added, calling it “a consequential moment” for the campus.
Members of The Staff and Student Body Have Spoken Out Following The Allegations
Over seventy members of the Cornell community left comments on the proposed resolution. One user, who chose to remain anonymous, said, “I support this resolution because it is a starting place. Not a false apology, slow-moving task force, or settlement payout. It says: we have a problem that needs solving.”
Another user, who also chose to remain anonymous, added, “What Jane Doe’s case has revealed are the many ways that the university failed in this respect. We saw conflicts of interest in the handling of both criminal and Title IX matters by internal Cornell departments that ultimately report to administrators whose primary focus is on maintaining relationships with funders and the bottom line, rather than student wellbeing.”
They went on to say, “We need a fresh start. This can only happen by acknowledging where things went wrong. We need to hold our leadership accountable so that they can take a good hard look at their missteps and declare to the world that Cornell will do better.”

None of the men involved have faced criminal charges at the time of this writing; however, the university has faced strong backlash for how it handled the allegations. As the Cornell Daily Sun first reported on September 18, President Michael Kotlikoff waited more than two weeks to publicly address the case. However, Cornell’s Board of Trustees continues to stand behind him.

Cornell faculty declares 'no confidence' in university leadership
November 7, 2026
Cornell University's Faculty Senate approved a resolution on Friday declaring "no confidence" in the administration's ability to handle what it has called a sexual assault crisis on campus.
The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to Faculty Senate members on Friday afternoon.
What's behind the resolution?
The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators have done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university.
The university leadership has faced intense criticism since mid-September when a former student, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in court documents, filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.
All seven men mentioned in the lawsuit have denied her allegations, saying the sex was consensual or that they weren't involved.
After learning about the case, Cornell closed the fraternity chapter and disciplined several students, without any criminal charges being filed.
The allegations were initially investigated by the campus police, which then passed its initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who did not prosecute — a decision that was later met with widespread criticism.
The investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York's attorney general.
What did the board chair say about the faculty vote?
Some faculty members have criticized University President Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school's disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.
The faculty body has no power over the university's top leaders but the resolution's backers had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell's trustees to address longstanding institutional failures they identified.
After the faculty vote, Cornell Board Chair Anne Smalling said it "reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable."
But she also expressed the board of trustees' support for President Kotlikoff and the administration.
"We support President Kotlikoff's commitment to taking all necessary steps to ensure students are safe on campus and working together as a community to help prevent this from happening again."
Resolution 'only the beginning'
Kotlikoff has yet to respond to the outcome of the faculty vote.
Under university procedures, the president has 30 days to respond in writing, a university spokesperson said.
Kotlikoff said the day before voting began on October 29 that faculty discussion and debate were "an important component of Cornell's shared governance."
He also pointed out that the university had taken measures including adding staff to its civil rights office, expanding sexual assault prevention education, and hiring staff focused on victim advocacy.
Iris Packman, a co-sponsor of the no-confidence resolution, told the Associated Press on Friday that the vote was "only the beginning" and that faculty would push for sweeping reforms.
Yasmeen Masoud, a Cornell junior who spoke Friday at a news conference organized by the resolution's sponsors, called the vote encouraging for students frustrated with the university's response.
"We should not have to beg for answers, demand basic transparency or generate media attention just to get our concerns acknowledged," she said. "It reminds us that there are people across this university who care deeply about its future and are willing to stand together to demand a better Cornell."

sources.news_title: Cornell faculty vote no confidence in university leadership
sources.text:
A governing body of Cornell University professors and instructors passed a vote of no confidence in university leadership over its handling of sexual assault, as rape allegations by a former student roil the Ivy League school.
The Cornell Faculty Senate on Friday approved a resolution expressing “no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault,” according to a statement from the university.
The vote is largely symbolic because the faculty body doesn’t have the authority to remove Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff. While it reflects growing dissatisfaction with the school’s leadership, the board of trustees signaled they back Kotlikoff in the wake of a lawsuit by the former student. In September, the woman — identified in court papers as Jane Doe — alleged in a civil lawsuit that she was assaulted by members of a campus fraternity about two years ago. She further alleged the university, the fraternity and her sorority failed to protect her.
“Today’s Faculty Senate vote reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable,” said Anne Meinig Smalling, the chair of the board of trustees, in the statement. “We support President Kotlikoff’s commitment to taking all necessary steps to ensure students are safe on campus and working together as a community to help prevent this from happening again.”
Cornell’s response to her allegations has drawn widespread criticism from politicians, faculty, students and alumni, many of whom have faulted Kotlikoff’s response and raised broad concerns about campus culture and sexual-assault protocols from far beyond the elite university’s base in Ithaca, New York.
Kotlikoff, who is in his mid-70s, has apologized and acknowledged shortcomings in Cornell’s response. At a meeting in mid-October with the Cornell Faculty Senate, Kotlikoff addressed calls for his resignation and pledged to make Cornell a leader in preventing and responding to sexual violence.
“If this university feels that they will solve this problem by replacing a president, that, itself, is not good for Cornell’s reputation, because I don’t think it’s the right way you address situations like this,” Kotlikoff said during the meeting to faculty senators who were deliberating the no-confidence vote.
The faculty senate’s decision follows calls to revamp the university’s culture and leadership.
In late October, Cornell’s chapter of the American Association of University Professors called for the resignation of Kotlikoff and vice president for student and campus life Ryan Lombardi, along with the “immediate suspension” of fraternities sponsored by the Interfraternity Council. The association, which also lacks authority to force the resignation, says it represents Cornell faculty, librarians and other academic staff, but doesn’t disclose membership numbers.
Kotlikoff, who became Cornell’s interim president in 2024, became president the following year as college campuses across the country were embroiled in controversy over the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the ensuing war in Gaza. Since then, the leadership of many large U.S. universities has rapidly turned over.

sources.news_title: Cornell Faculty Votes No Confidence in Administration
sources.text:
Cornell University's Faculty Senate voted Friday to declare no confidence in the university's central administration over its handling of sexual assault, after a former student's allegation that she was drugged and gang raped at a fraternity house in 2024 became a national story. Seventy-five members voted for the resolution, 50 voted against, five abstained and five did not vote, according to its co-sponsors. The resolution does not call for President Michael Kotlikoff to resign, and the board of trustees said within hours that it remains confident in him.
The text says the Faculty Senate "has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University." The co-sponsors called the vote "a reckoning for our University" and said faculty had come together despite what they described as repeated attempts by the administration to silence them. They said they want the university to address the roots of what they called rape culture on campus and the ways Title IX procedures have been used against survivors. The vote is symbolic and gives the senate no power to remove the president or any administrator.
The board of trustees responded the same day. Board Chair Anne Meinig Smalling said the vote reflects deep anger across campus and shows that what happened to the former student, who is identified in court papers as Jane Doe, is unacceptable, and that there is no place for sexual violence at Cornell. She said the board nonetheless remains confident that Kotlikoff and his administration are the right leaders to address sexual assault on campus, and the university said it would make no changes to its leadership. Jane Doe said in a statement that she believes the senate did not reach its decision lightly and considered all available information.
The allegation became public in mid-September, when the woman filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at the fraternity house in October 2024. She was 20 at the time. The university disciplined several of the accused after a months-long Title IX investigation, and reports say only two of the seven were expelled. Chi Phi's chapter at Cornell was suspended in November 2024, and the fraternity's national organization says it expelled the accused members within days of the police report. No one has been charged, and lawyers for at least two of the men have denied the allegations.
The criminal case has moved out of local hands. The Tompkins County district attorney initially concluded that the encounter was consensual and brought no charges, a decision that drew scrutiny after a campus police interview transcript surfaced in which the woman said she was confident she had been raped, and which the prosecutor says he never received. Gov. Kathy Hochul removed the district attorney from the case and appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor, saying police and prosecutors had failed to protect the woman. This week James named Jacqueline Kelly, a former federal sex-crimes prosecutor described as a Cornell alumna, to lead the criminal investigation and report to her office. Four of the men named in the lawsuit have joined an effort to have James removed from the case, arguing that she posted a message supporting the woman on social media before she was appointed, and Jane Doe's legal team has continued its fight despite Kelly's appointment.
Cornell has commissioned its own review. Sally Yates, the former U.S. deputy attorney general, is leading an independent investigation into how the university responded to the woman's 2024 report and into its procedures for handling similar reports from other students. Some professors had argued that the faculty should wait for her findings before voting, and the resolution passed before any report has been released. The university has not said when it will publish her conclusions in the reporting reviewed.
The vote follows weeks of campus protest that began after the case became national news. Kotlikoff has said the way the university handled the 2024 matter is itself a subject of inquiry, and in an October video called what happened to the woman deeply disturbing, as reported in HNGN's earlier coverage of the independent review. Students held a seven-hour sit-in in early October, and a separate rally outside the administration building called for stronger sanctions in assault cases and enforceable investigation timelines.
The immediate question is whether a symbolic vote changes anything when the governing board has already said it will not act. The faculty has now put its position on the record, but the decisions that will determine the outcome belong to others: the attorney general's office, which must decide whether to bring charges, and Yates, whose report will test whether the university's process or only its results failed. Until both arrive, Cornell is governed by a president the faculty does not trust and a board that does.

Cornell faculty vote ‘no confidence’ in university leadership
Cornell University's Faculty Senate approved a resolution Friday declaring “no confidence” in the school's top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a former student's lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024.
The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to Faculty Senate members on Friday afternoon.
The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators handled the woman’s allegations properly and have done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university.
Related video above: 'You deserve to be safe': bipartisan campus safety bill promises help for survivors
While the faculty body has no power over the university's top leaders, backers of the resolution had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell's trustees to address longstanding institutional failures they identified.
Board of Trustees Chair Anne Smalling said in a statement the faculty vote “reflects the deep anger across our campus” and sent a clear signal that what happened to the woman was unacceptable, but added that Kotlikoff and his administration were the right leaders to “thoughtfully and comprehensively” address the issue.
Thomas Giuffra, an attorney for the woman who filed the lawsuit, said in a statement Friday that “we are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus.”
Lawsuit sparked outrage on campus
The Cornell community has been distressed since mid-September, when a former student, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in court documents, filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024.
All of the men have denied her allegations, saying the sex was consensual or that they weren’t involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York’s attorney general.
Cornell disciplined several of the accused students following a monthslong Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write “reflection” papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by The New York Times.
Kotlikoff also convened a task force to study the problem of sexual misconduct on campus, which released certain recommendations.
Some faculty members have criticized Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school's disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture.
Paul Ortiz, a labor history professor who co-sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said last week that hundreds of students, staff, alumni and faculty approached the resolution’s sponsors to emphasize that “the Jane Doe case is but a tip of the iceberg” and that “a veritable fortress of silence has been breached” around sexual violence since the resolution’s introduction.
Cornell's president defended his leadership
Speaking to Faculty Senate members on the first day that they debated the no-confidence resolution, Kotlikoff pledged to make the university a leader in addressing sexual assault and asked for more time to make changes.
Kotlikoff defended his leadership, arguing that replacing him would do little to solve complex problems and could damage Cornell’s reputation. He acknowledged he had not read the campus police report, explaining that university policy barred top administrators from interfering in criminal investigations. He also rejected suggestions he had been indifferent to the woman’s case, though he acknowledged only recently learning she had left Cornell.
Kotlikoff said the university needed to determine whether fraternities could operate safely and left open the possibility of sweeping restrictions on Greek life. He argued that decisions should be based on research and evidence rather than emotion.
Some professors had said faculty should wait to vote until the release of an independent investigation by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, whom the university hired to examine how Cornell responded to the woman's initial rape report in 2024 and its overall procedures for handling similar reports from other students.
Yasmeen Masoud, a Cornell junior who spoke Friday at a news conference organized by the resolution’s sponsors, called the vote encouraging for students frustrated with the university’s response.
“We should not have to beg for answers, demand basic transparency or generate media attention just to get our concerns acknowledged,” she said. “It reminds us that there are people across this university who care deeply about its future and are willing to stand together to demand a better Cornell.”
Iris Packman, a co-sponsor of the no-confidence resolution, said Friday that the vote was “only the beginning” and that faculty would push for sweeping reforms.
The no-confidence resolution did not call for Kotlikoff’s resignation.

The Yates investigation is just one of several efforts to re-examine the case and the way local and university officials handled the matter.
The Tompkins County District Attorney’s office has also faced intense public criticism for prosecutors’ decision in 2024 not to pursue criminal charges against the men named in the September civil lawsuit.
